one_liner: Low-level, zero-copy, race-free C++17 file and memory-map i/o library; no head-to-head numbers against POSIX read/write.
what_it_does: LLFIO is a portable file i/o and filesystem library (the former Boost.AFIO v2 and the abandoned WG21 P1031 proposal) built around a hierarchy of handle types: path_handle, directory_handle, file_handle, mapped_file_handle, section_handle and map_handle. It gives noexcept scatter-gather reads and writes returning Outcome result types, anchored race-free (no TOCTOU) path opens, byte-range and shared filesystem mutexes, deadlines and cancellation, and generic filesystem algorithms (directory traversal, summary, reliable deletion, content cloning). It replaces raw POSIX/Win32 calls or std::fstream and std::filesystem with a different interface; it is not a drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: The design target is near-zero software overhead per i/o: no malloc, no exceptions and no whole-machine memory copy on the i/o path, path_view instead of allocated std::filesystem::path, and thin wrappers over pread/pwrite-style syscalls (the README says about 100 ns per i/o on Linux, syscall included). It exposes O_DIRECT and seven kernel caching modes, plus memory-mapped scatter-gather i/o with large and huge page support, so you can pick the caching and copy behaviour per handle. It does not add a faster algorithm on top of the OS; the gain is avoiding the allocation, copying and locking that iostreams and std::filesystem add.
when_to_use: Storage engines or databases that do 4 KiB direct (O_DIRECT) i/o on NVMe or Optane and need per-op overhead well under the device latency.
Portable code across Linux, Windows and FreeBSD that wants memory-mapped files, sparse files, hole punching and large/huge pages through one API.
Filesystem algorithms that must be race-free against concurrent renames (anchored path_handle opens, no stored paths).
Builds with exceptions and RTTI disabled that still need rich error codes (original NT kernel error codes are preserved).
when_not_to_use: You need an async submission-queue backend: Linux io_uring support is still on the README's todo list and multiplex.hpp is only an interface sketch; use liburing or SPDK directly.
You want a measured speedup over read/write or std::fstream: the project publishes overhead and device latency figures only, never a comparison against another library.
Mac OS deployments: the README says it is less well tested there.
Header-only use on Windows without status_code or a shared ntkernel error category: Build.md warns error-code comparisons can randomly fail.
Small tools that just read a few files: the API surface is large and the build pulls in QuickCppLib and Outcome via a CMake bootstrap.

integration.form: header-only, static lib or shared lib (selectable; also vcpkg 'llfio' and prebuilt release binaries)
integration.dependencies: QuickCppLib and Outcome (fetched by the CMake bootstrap); git submodules ntkernel-error-category and wg14_signals; an STL with working <filesystem>
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 with std::filesystem; CMake 3.9+; CI covers GCC and Clang on Linux, Xcode, Visual Studio (Android NDK and MinGW build only)
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows, FreeBSD, Mac OS (less tested), Android/iOS build-only; README targets kernels back to Linux 2.6.32 and Windows 8.1
integration.thread_safety: not documented per handle; the v2 redesign removed all internal use of multiple threads and shared_ptr, so synchronise shared handles yourself

gotchas: Header-only mode on Windows can produce binaries where semantic error-code comparisons fail; define LLFIO_EXPERIMENTAL_STATUS_CODE=1 or link the prebuilt library.
map_handle's page cache does not self-trim; you must call trim_cache() or allocations accumulate.
Open Windows bugs: mapped_temp_inode leaks space (#160) and map(section, reserve) does not work (#121); algorithm::traverse relies on vector<list<move-only>> (#98).
Clone with --recursive and do an out-of-tree build or the CMake build fails; Build.md itself is flagged as inaccurate for POSIX (#111).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LLFIO over liburing or SPDK when you want a portable, synchronous, race-free file and mmap abstraction across Linux and Windows rather than a Linux-only async queue; for raw IOPS at high queue depth liburing or SPDK are the measured options. Unlike FastMap or UMap it does not replace the kernel mmap path, it wraps it.
verified_claims_summary: The README gives about 100 ns of software overhead per i/o on Linux and 99th-percentile QD1 4 KiB direct read latencies of 30 us (Linux), 37 us (Windows) and 70 us (FreeBSD) on NVMe, set beside manufacturer device latencies; no baseline library, compiler, flags or exact hardware are tied to those figures. The repo's fs_probe_results.yaml carries raw latency profiles (for example AMD Threadripper PRO 5975WX, Linux 5.15, RAID0 Samsung PM9A1 on XFS: direct QD1 4 KiB read p99 about 96 us), which are device characterisations, not comparisons.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-08-24), dual Apache-2.0/BSL-1.0, mature and in production use per the README, but the standardisation effort was abandoned in 2025 and io_uring remains unimplemented.
